walkthroughs.body_html:
Nature & Variety of Living Organisms — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Nature & Variety of Living Organisms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Nature & Variety of Living Organisms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: How does myelination increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction?
options: Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), skipping the myelinated sections.
Myelin makes the axon thicker so the signal travels faster through more material.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.

mcqs.q: What is the role of DNA ligase when inserting a gene into a plasmid?
options: It forms phosphodiester bonds that join the gene to the cut plasmid, sealing the recombinant DNA.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
DNA ligase reads the gene and translates it into protein.
DNA ligase cuts the plasmid open so the gene can be inserted.

mcqs.q: Why is negative feedback the default mechanism in homeostasis?
options: It opposes deviations from a set point, returning the variable toward its normal value — keeping internal conditions stable.
Negative feedback only operates when something goes wrong in the body.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
Negative feedback amplifies changes to make them more noticeable.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Stem cell”?
options: Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Specialised cells”?
options: A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Eukaryotic cell”?
options: Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Subcellular structures”?
options: A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Cell”?
options: A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.

options: Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
